meta.title: Who really said "I’ve Had a Perfectly Wonderful Evening, But This Wasn’t It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Groucho. The gag is in print from June 1935 — six years before the first Groucho credit — and Groucho denied it in 1962. Its author is unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I've Had a Perfectly Wonderful Evening, But This Wasn't It'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous 1935 film-serialization gag. Reader’s Digest pinned it on Groucho in 1941; he denied ever saying it in 1962.

answer.label: Not Groucho Marx — a 1935 gag he denied making
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known appearance is a newspaper serialization of the MGM film No More Ladies, printed 20 June 1935, in which a departing guest says ‘I had a lovely evening but this wasn’t it’ — with no author named. Groucho was not connected to the line until March 1941, when Reader’s Digest ran it on a contribution from Eddie Cantor, and in 1962 Groucho wrote in print that he never made the remark in real life.

source.excerpt: She dropped a kiss on Fanny’s forehead. “Good night sweet. If you see Sherry tell him I had a lovely evening but this wasn’t it.”
trail: The earliest instance Quote Investigator has located is the 20 June 1935 serialization of No More Ladies in an Iowa newspaper, where the line is spoken by a character and credited to nobody the full citation chain ↗.

Through the later 1930s the gag circulated under other names entirely: the Hollywood columnist Sidney Skolsky credited the comedian Hugh Herbert in October 1936, an unnamed young man was given it in November 1936, and in 1940 Skolsky printed it again — this time crediting the actor Walter Catlett Skolsky’s two versions ↗.

The first attribution to Groucho is Reader’s Digest, March 1941, carrying a footnote that credits the performer Eddie Cantor as the contributor — six years after the line was already in print the 1941 citation ↗.

Groucho disclaimed it himself in a 1962 newspaper-supplement piece: ‘Cross my heart, I never made that mean remark in real life.’ Quote Investigator accepts the denial, while noting it leaves open the possibility he used the quip in a routine — for which no direct evidence has been found Groucho’s own denial ↗.
source.excerptNote: The line is spoken by a character in a newspaper serialization of the film, adapted by Beatrice Faber from A. E. Thomas’s stage play. Quote Investigator notes that Rachel Crothers, Edith Fitzgerald and George Oppenheimer all worked on the screenplay, that any of them might have contributed the quip, and that it does not know whether the line was in the original play — so the author is genuinely unidentified rather than merely unrecorded.
source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status here, because the gag has no identified author. Its earliest known printing is an anonymous 1935 newspaper serialization, and the wording that circulates under Groucho’s name is a later variant, closer to the Reader’s Digest form of 1941 than to that 1935 text — though it matches neither exactly. With no attributable source work we cannot responsibly call it public domain. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Groucho Marx
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Groucho
author.metaLine: 1890–1977 · American comedian, actor and game-show host
author.bio: Groucho Marx was the great master of the one-line retort, which makes him a natural home for any orphaned put-down — and this one fits his register so exactly that the credit has never needed evidence. He is unusual among quote magnets in having answered the charge directly: in a 1962 magazine piece he disclaimed this one outright, under a section headed ‘Groucho didn’t say it’.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A rare case where the man himself filed a denial. The line was already six years old and had been credited to at least three other people before Groucho’s name landed on it.

items.why: Writing in This Week Magazine in March 1962, Groucho disclaimed the quip under a section headed ‘Groucho didn’t say it’: ‘Cross my heart, I never made that mean remark in real life.’ his 1962 piece ↗
The Hollywood columnist gave the line to Herbert leaving a party — five years before Groucho was named. Skolsky then reassigned it himself the 1936 column ↗

items.who: Credited by the same columnist in 1940
items.why: In Cosmopolitan, Skolsky called it ‘the best line ever pulled at a Hollywood party’ and attributed it to Catlett. One columnist, two different names, four years apart the 1940 citation ↗
The line appears in a character’s dialogue in the serialized No More Ladies. Quote Investigator names five people who could have written it and declines to choose the earliest citation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous 1935 gag that acquired Groucho’s name in 1941, and which Groucho himself publicly disowned in 1962 the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to him
lead: The joke is a paraprosdokian — a sentence that sets up one expectation and demolishes it in the last three words. That structure was Groucho’s signature, so the line sounds like him even to people who have never seen a Marx Brothers film.

What makes the case unusual is the paper trail running the other way. Most misattributions are never contested by their supposed authors; this one was, by a man who had spent decades being credited with other people’s cracks and had evidently had enough.
detailsBody: The chain is unusually well documented for a joke. It surfaces in a 1935 newspaper serialization of a film, gets handed to a comedian in 1936 and to an actor in 1940 by the same columnist, and only reaches Groucho in 1941 — via Reader’s Digest, sourced to Eddie Cantor rather than to Groucho himself.

Quote Investigator’s conclusion is careful: Groucho may well have used the line in a routine, and no evidence has been found either way. What the record does not support is the anecdote everybody tells — Groucho delivering the insult to a real hostess on a real evening.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known instance is the 20 June 1935 Bedford Times-Press serialization of No More Ladies, reading "I had a lovely evening but this wasn’t it."
Sidney Skolsky credited Hugh Herbert (Oct 1936) and later Walter Catlett (1940) with the same line.
Reader's Digest, March 1941, first attached the quip to Groucho Marx, contributed by Eddie Cantor.
In 1962 Groucho wrote "Cross my heart, I never made that mean remark in real life."
Wikiquote’s Groucho Marx page does not list this quip in its Misattributed section.
No More Ladies is a 1935 MGM film.
